scribe_response.text: Can you tell me about the home you grew up in? I was born in nineteen forty-eight in a terraced house on Hollin Road in Leeds. It was a two up two down, um and the front door opened straight onto the pavement. My um father worked as a signalman for the railway, and my mother took in sewing. My brother Peter was four years older than me and never let um me forget it. We shared um the back bedroom until I was nine, with a curtain on a string between us. The kitchen was the heart of the house, with a black range that my mother polished every Friday. She used a tin of blacklead and a stiff brush, and she hummed hymns throughout. There was a pegged uh rug before the fire that she had made from old coat cuttings. In winter the windows grew ferns of frost on the inside, and we dressed under the blankets. The lavatory was out in the yard, so nobody lingered there in January. On Mondays the whole street smelled, street smelled of wet wool and carbolic soap, because it was washday. My mother had a dolly tub, a mangle with great wooden rollers, and arms like a docker. I was allowed to turn the mangle handle, which I thought a tremendous honour. What happened next? Sheets hung across uh the uh yard on a line propped up with a long forked pole. If it rained they came indoors and steamed above the range on a wooden airer. Her sewing machine was a Singer with a treadle under the front window. She made wedding dresses, school pinafores, pinafores and the odd black coat for funerals. Pins lived in a velvet tomato on the sideboard, and I was forbidden to touch it. Of course I um touched it, and I still carry a little scar on my thumb. My father came home at six in the morning or the evening, depending on his shift. He smelled of coal smoke uh and Woodbine cigarettes, and he carried a tin box of sandwiches. Sometimes he took me to the signal box on a Sunday, and I climbed the steep wooden stairs. Inside were great iron levers painted red and yellow, and a brass bell. He let me pull one lever once, and I felt as though I had moved the whole of Yorkshire. Our street ended at a wall, and beyond it ran the railway cutting, full of rosebay willowherb. Peter and I collected train numbers in a penny notebook. Next uh door lived Missus Pickersgill, who kept a canary called Gladstone and had a very sharp tongue. Can you tell me more about that? She gave us a humbug each if we swept her step without being asked. On the other side lived the Dawsons, uh who had seven children and one tin um bath between them. Saturday night was bath night, and ours was filled from the copper in the corner of the kitchen. Peter went first because um he was the eldest, and I always got the lukewarm water. Afterwards we sat by the range with cocoa and dripping toast. My mother cut my hair herself with the dressmaking scissors, and my fringe was never straight. We had no garden, only a yard, but my, my father grew tomatoes in an old uh tin bath by the wall. He treated them like patients, checking each truss and talking to them in a low voice. I think that was where my love of growing things began. On summer evenings the street filled with children skipping and bowling hoops. The coalman came on Thursdays with his horse, Duke, and I fed him crusts. When I close my eyes I can still smell the uh blacklead, the wet wool and the toast. It was a small house with very little money in it, but nothing ever felt lacking. My mother used to say that a tidy house and a warm kettle would see you through anything.
